result: For additive space-time white noise the scheme achieves mean-square convergence rates arbitrarily close to 1/2 in space and 1/4 in time, with slower rates for rougher noise.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous strong convergence rates for a fully discrete approximation of the stochastic Burgers equation, with rates degrading as noise regularity decreases.

title: Elastic Wave Imaging Via Kirchhoff Migration: Resolution Analysis And Inclusion Identification
authors: Josselin Garnier Zetao Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the inverse problem of determining the location, orientation, shape, and material parameters of a small elastic inclusion embedded in a homogeneous medium from full-aperture measurements of the scattered field. Using a small-volume expansion, we derive explicit leading-order expressions for four Kirchhoff migration imaging functionals, denoted by PP, PS, SP, and SS, corresponding to the four combinations of pressure (P) and shear (S) waves used for receiver- and source-side backpropagation. The resulting point-spread functions quantitatively characterize the resolution of each mode and show that the SS mode achieves the highest spatial resolution. For an elliptic inclusion, we show that the PP mode uniquely determines the elastic moment tensor (EMT) within the leading-order asymptotic model, thereby enabling the reconstruction of the material and geometric parameters of the inclusion. For a general small scatterer, the reconstruction may instead be interpreted as an effective elliptic representation determined by its leading-order EMT. For a disk, the parameter-identification problem is underdetermined; nevertheless, explicit upper and lower bounds on its volume are derived. We further analyze the model error arising from neglected cross-mode contributions when the distance from the center of the measurement configuration is not sufficiently large relative to the elastic wavelengths. Numerical experiments support the theoretical predictions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed imaging and reconstruction methods.
tldr: Kirchhoff migration functionals for PP, PS, SP and SS elastic waves are analyzed to characterize resolution and identify small elastic inclusions from scattered-field measurements.
motivation: Determining the location, orientation, shape and material parameters of a small elastic inclusion from full-aperture scattered-field data is a classical inverse-scattering problem in elastic wave imaging.
method: A small-volume expansion yields explicit leading-order point-spread functions for four Kirchhoff migration imaging functionals built from P- and S-wave backpropagation, with an analysis of model error from neglected cross-mode contributions.
result: The SS mode gives the highest spatial resolution; the PP mode uniquely fixes the elastic moment tensor for an elliptic inclusion, while for a disk the identification is underdetermined but explicit volume bounds are derived.
conclusion: The theory is validated by numerical experiments, showing effective imaging and parameter reconstruction, and provides quantitative resolution limits for elastic migration imaging.

title: A Structured-Surrogate Double-Model Approach To Regularization Parameter Selection
authors: Malena Espa\~nol, Markus Juvonen, Samuli Siltanen, Ilaria Trombini, Chuyang Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Double-model methods select a regularization parameter by matching the discrepancy between two reconstructions of the same data to a prescribed target. The Structured-Surrogate Double-Model (SSDM) framework is developed around a computationally inexpensive structured surrogate of the forward operator and a spectrally explicit perturbation, with the selected parameter subsequently applied to the original inverse problem. Given a prescribed target, parameter selection requires neither prior knowledge of the noise level nor training data. For a class of Tikhonov regularization problems, the squared discrepancy is shown to attain a strict maximum at zero regularization, decay as [MATH], and decrease strictly beyond an explicit phase-aware threshold. A complementary, data-dependent certificate is established to guarantee strict monotonicity on finite intervals, enabling unique and reliable target matching even when the global threshold is overly conservative. The discrepancy is further connected to directional roughness in image deblurring, providing a geometric interpretation of the selection principle. Experiments on synthetic images and on synthetically blurred natural photographs illustrate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical applicability of certified parameter selection.
tldr: The paper introduces a Structured-Surrogate Double-Model (SSDM) framework for selecting Tikhonov regularization parameters by matching the discrepancy between two reconstructions to a prescribed target.
motivation: Classical regularization parameter selection typically requires knowledge of the noise level or training data, which is often unavailable in practical inverse problems.
method: A computationally cheap structured surrogate of the forward operator, combined with a spectrally explicit perturbation, is used to define a discrepancy whose behavior (strict maximum at zero regularization, decay, and monotone decrease beyond an explicit threshold) is analyzed theoretically, plus a data-dependent certificate for strict monotonicity on finite intervals.
result: The squared discrepancy is proven to attain a strict maximum at zero regularization and to decrease strictly past a phase-aware threshold; experiments on synthetic images and synthetically blurred natural photographs confirm the theory and the practical value of certified parameter selection.
conclusion: SSDM enables reliable, training-free and noise-level-free regularization parameter selection with theoretical guarantees, illustrated in image deblurring.

title: The Multiplier Step Size In Classical Two-block Admm: Convergence And Counterexamples
authors: Benqi Liu, Qiming Dai, Zaiwen Wen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How large can the multiplier step be in the classical two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)? We keep the penalty fixed and use the usual primal updates. We consider finite-dimensional problems with closed proper convex objectives. We assume that a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker point exists and that each block subproblem attains its minimum at every step. Under these assumptions, the constraint images and the multiplier converge for a range of factors that extends beyond the golden ratio. The constraint matrices may be rank deficient. For larger steps, we construct two fixed compact polytopes and give an explicit threshold below two. The polytopes admit an infeasible periodic orbit for every factor at or above this threshold. At that threshold, ADMM can cycle even for smooth strongly convex objectives. This gives a negative answer to Glowinski's question about the full interval from zero to two. A different pair of piecewise-quadratic objectives gives geometrically growing residuals. For the general convex class, we locate the endpoint of the uniform convergence interval near 1.88688256. A convergence certificate on the unit circle gives the lower bound, while a separate periodic orbit gives the upper bound. Exact arithmetic verifies that the two bounds differ by less than 0.000000174.
tldr: The paper determines the exact endpoint (~1.88688256) of the uniform convergence interval for the multiplier step size in classical two-block ADMM and constructs periodic-orbit counterexamples for larger steps.
motivation: Glowinski's question asked whether two-block ADMM converges for the full multiplier step interval (0, 2); this work aims to settle the true boundary of guaranteed convergence.
method: Assuming a KKT point exists and subproblems are solved exactly, the authors prove convergence of constraint images and multipliers for step factors beyond the golden ratio, construct fixed compact polytopes admitting infeasible periodic orbits, and use a convergence certificate on the unit circle plus exact arithmetic.
result: Convergence is established up to a threshold near 1.88688256, above which explicit periodic orbits (and even smooth strongly convex examples) can cycle or produce geometrically growing residuals, with lower and upper bounds matching to within 1.74e-7.
conclusion: The full (0,2) interval conjectured by Glowinski does not yield convergence; the paper sharply locates the uniform convergence endpoint for general closed proper convex two-block ADMM.

title: I Don't Care How You Hide It, I Care What You Do: Runtime Detection Of Malicious Ml Models
authors: Andrew Case Hala Ali
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pre-trained machine learning (ML) models shared through public platforms can be weaponized to execute malicious payloads during loading or inference. Existing scanners prove inadequate for detecting malicious models as they rely on static analysis and function denylists, support limited serialization formats, and miss attacks that replace denylisted functions with equivalent alternatives, exploit unsupported loading paths, or abuse legitimate framework APIs. To address this problem, we present ModelShield, the first runtime behavioral detection system for malicious ML models that attributes observed system-level behavior to specific model operations. It combines application-level instrumentation of ML framework APIs with eBPF-based syscall tracing, tracking model behavior across spawned threads and processes to separate model-triggered activity from environment noise. Attributed syscall sequences are classified using 195 detection patterns mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. We implemented ModelShield to support 17 ML frameworks and 36 formats. On an independent dataset, it is the only evaluated tool to achieve zero false positives, with false negatives limited to payloads that produce no malicious runtime behavior. It detected all 29 published evasion variants spanning function substitution, loading-path obfuscation, and TensorFlow API abuse, where no existing scanner achieved complete coverage. Across 145,000 models scanned from public platforms, it captured 41 malicious models on Hugging Face, including a reverse-shell payload and a payload that performed host reconnaissance and outbound exfiltration. Among these, ModelScan, PickleScan, Fickling, and ModelAudit detected only 29%, 56%, 80%, and 93%, respectively. Despite runtime overhead, ModelShield has a median analysis time of 12.3 seconds, with 90% of scans completing within 35.5 seconds, making it practical for hub-scale screening.
tldr: ModelShield is a runtime behavioral detection system that identifies malicious pre-trained ML models by attributing system-level activity to model operations.
motivation: Publicly shared ML models can execute malicious payloads during loading or inference, and existing scanners relying on static analysis and denylists miss evasive attacks.
method: The system combines ML framework API instrumentation with eBPF syscall tracing, tracks activity across threads/processes, and classifies attributed syscall sequences using 195 detection patterns mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.
result: It achieves zero false positives on an independent dataset, detects all 29 evasion variants, and finds 41 malicious models among 145,000 public models, outperforming existing scanners.
conclusion: Runtime behavioral monitoring is practical for hub-scale screening and more robust than static scanners for detecting malicious ML models.

title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
authors: Daniil Filienko, Anusha Bagalkotkar, Xan Vongsathorn, Sikha Pentyala
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.
tldr: The paper introduces Ext-Classify-Priv, an audience-conditioned framework that extracts information types from a corpus, classifies which are private for a given audience under contextual integrity, and protects only those via anonymization or Feature-DP synthetic data generation.
motivation: Existing differentially private synthetic text generation and anonymization methods ignore downstream usage context, applying uniform privacy guarantees and losing useful information, even though sensitivity is audience-dependent.
method: A three-stage pipeline extracts information types from the corpus, classifies their privacy status per audience following contextual integrity, and then applies anonymization or Feature-DP-based synthetic text generation only to the sensitive attributes identified.
result: On Reddit data with three audiences, audience-specific releases are more faithful than an audience-agnostic release for every audience; on bioRxiv, MAUVE improves from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1, and on proprietary real estate data anonymization raises MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959.
conclusion: Conditioning privacy protection on the intended audience yields more faithful and useful data releases than audience-agnostic differential privacy or attribute-category anonymization.

title: Optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming: Complexity And Implementations
authors: Damiano Azzolini, Giuseppe Mazzotta, Francesco Ricca, Fabrizio Riguzzi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) extends Answer Set Programming with the possibility of representing uncertain data. Among the possible available semantics, we focus here on the credal semantics. In this setting, prior work has focused exclusively on plain ASP programs, i.e., programs without optimization constructs. However, many real world tasks define optimality criteria over the possible solutions, which cannot be conveniently modeled with existing probabilistic ASP frameworks. In this paper, we close this gap and propose optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming, which extends PASP by also allowing weak constraints, which are the standard optimization construct of ASP. We define the semantics of such programs, study the computational complexity of the inference and most probable explanation tasks, and propose practical implementations based on Algebraic Model Counting and Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers. An empirical evaluation of the proposed approach on three real world tasks confirms the applicability of our framework.
tldr: The paper introduces optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming by extending credal-semantics PASP with weak constraints, and studies its complexity and implementations.
motivation: Existing probabilistic ASP frameworks lack optimization constructs, making it hard to model real-world tasks that require optimality criteria over possible solutions.
method: The authors define semantics for optimal PASP with weak constraints, analyze the computational complexity of inference and most probable explanation tasks, and implement solvers using Algebraic Model Counting and ASP with Quantifiers.
result: They characterize the complexity of inference and MPE, and empirical evaluation on three real-world tasks demonstrates the applicability of the proposed framework.
conclusion: Optimal PASP closes a gap in probabilistic ASP by supporting weak constraints, with practical implementations showing feasibility for real-world optimization tasks.

title: Fair Selection Of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
authors: Sophie Hall, Heinrich H. Nax, Saverio Bolognani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.
tldr: This tutorial analyzes equilibrium selection in generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems through a social-choice lens, arguing that the conventional variational GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability and proposing a fair GNE (f-GNE) that optimizes a fairness metric matched to the available comparability.
motivation: GNE problems admit a continuum of equilibria, so implementations must select one; this selection determines how shared-constraint costs are distributed, and the widely used v-GNE is often assumed fair without justification.
method: The authors borrow comparability notions from social choice theory to characterize what inter-agent cost comparability each selection rule presupposes, then construct the f-GNE by explicitly optimizing a corresponding fairness metric, with constructive computation for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games.
result: The GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability, whereas v-GNE implicitly demands cardinal unit comparability; f-GNE provides a comparability-matched, fairness-optimizing selection, illustrated via an electric-vehicle charging game.
conclusion: Equilibrium selection should be made explicit and aligned with the comparability assumptions one is willing to make, offering a principled fairness-aware alternative to default v-GNE selection.

title: Path Isolation And Reachability In Surface-Embedded Graphs With Restricted Cycle And Cut Structure
authors: Neelabjo Shubhashis Choudhury, Chetan Gupta, Raghunath Tewari
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the reachability problem in directed surface-embedded graphs under two structural restrictions, using isolating weight assignments. First, we consider graphs whose underlying undirected embeddings contain at most polynomially many simple surface non-separating cycles. We develop a polynomially bounded, logspace-computable skew-symmetric edge-weight assignment with nonzero circulation around every simple cycle. This yields an unambiguous logspace (UL) upper bound for directed reachability. The construction also gives an SPL upper bound for bipartite perfect matching in the corresponding undirected graph class. Second, for [MATH]-genus directed graphs admitting a balanced hierarchical genus decomposition with [MATH] crossing edges at every partition, we obtain an unambiguous [MATH]-space bound for reachability. Our approach combines path-isolating weights for lower-genus subgraphs using polynomially bounded FKS hashing refinements at successive merging levels.
tldr: The paper studies directed reachability in surface-embedded graphs using path-isolating weight assignments to obtain logspace and unambiguous complexity upper bounds.
motivation: Reachability in restricted graph classes is a central problem in computational complexity, and surface-embedded graphs provide a structured setting where isolating weights can yield better space bounds.
method: The authors construct polynomially bounded, logspace-computable skew-symmetric edge weights that isolate paths in graphs with limited surface non-separating cycles, and extend the approach to bounded-genus graphs via hierarchical decompositions and FKS hashing.
result: They obtain a UL upper bound for directed reachability in the restricted surface-embedded graph class, an SPL bound for bipartite perfect matching, and an unambiguous space bound for bounded-genus graphs with balanced hierarchical decompositions.
conclusion: The work advances the complexity-theoretic understanding of reachability in surface-embedded graphs through isolating weight techniques, but it is purely classical complexity theory and not connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: When Feedback Becomes A Backdoor: Tracing Backdoor Skill Formation In Text-Space Skill Optimization
authors: Louise Nayeong Koh, Yaechan Lee, Myeongjong Lee, Doyeon Kim, Juyoung Park, Seunggyu Kim, Inseo Kim, Chaerin Jung, Hyogon Ryu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reference answers are a supervision channel in text-space Skill optimization, which produces reusable text artifacts called Skills that guide future agent behavior. Poisoning those answers can induce a persistent trigger-conditioned rule without giving the attacker access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file. We study this reference-feedback poisoning in SkillOpt by tracing an attacker-supplied trigger--payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation. In SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, the natural attack retains an exact rule in all three seeds; each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered questions and 0/200 clean questions. In seed 42, removing the rule eliminates activation, and an in-run comparison shows similar clean accuracy to benign SkillOpt (169/200 versus 171/200). In SpreadsheetBench, where the payload requires an additional workbook edit, no natural run retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostic interventions locate two successive bottlenecks: the Analyst abstracts away required literals, and, once literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can remove exact edits before candidate construction. Poisoned references can therefore create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.
tldr: The paper traces how poisoning reference answers in text-space Skill optimization for LLM agents can implant persistent trigger-conditioned backdoor rules without access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file.
motivation: Reusable text 'Skills' guiding agent behavior introduce a supervision channel via reference answers, which the authors show is a plausible attack surface (reference-feedback poisoning) whose retention dynamics are not understood.
method: They study SkillOpt by tracing attacker-supplied trigger–payload mappings from the reflection stage to held-out activation, testing natural attacks on SearchQA and SpreadsheetBench across three seeds plus diagnostic interventions to isolate failure bottlenecks.
result: In SearchQA the attack retains an exact rule in all seeds, emitting the payload on 200/200 triggered and 0/200 clean questions with clean accuracy near benign SkillOpt (169 vs 171/200); in SpreadsheetBench no natural run retains the rule, with the Analyst abstracting literals and edit-budget ranking removing exact edits.
conclusion: Poisoned references can create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not guarantee the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.

title: Universal Decoding For Gaussian Mimo-isi: Spherical Ensembles And Symmetric Neighborhoods
authors: Meir Feder Nir Elkayam
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a universal decoder for cyclic Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output channels with intersymbol interference and unknown channel taps and spatial noise covariance. Codewords are drawn independently and uniformly from a sphere of fixed total energy. Under stated bounds on frequency variation, the decoder attains the ensemble-average error exponent of informed maximum-likelihood decoding for fixed channels and channels with growing memory. We approximate the frequency response by a constant matrix within each frequency block. For this auxiliary channel, every matched log-likelihood is affine in a common sufficient statistic. At fixed received output, we compute the statistic density of an independent competitor. The decoder selects the candidate with the smallest statistic density, equivalently minimizing a weighted sum of residual log-determinants. The density and its support volume give an upper bound on the universal competitor probability. Affinity ensures that at least half of a suitable symmetric neighborhood of the transmitted statistic has matched likelihood no smaller than that of the transmitted word. Integrating a density lower bound over this half gives the matched competitor bound. These bounds establish equality of error exponents, which a Gaussian channel comparison transfers to the original channel. The same decoder attains the matched exponent for independent frequency blocks with prescribed energies satisfying the stated conditions. For energies proportional to block length, an additional gain condition ensures that this exponent is at least that of the total-energy spherical ensemble.
tldr: The paper constructs a universal decoder for cyclic Gaussian MIMO channels with intersymbol interference and unknown channel taps/noise covariance, achieving informed maximum-likelihood error exponents for spherical code ensembles.
motivation: Universal decoding is needed when channel state information is unavailable, particularly for Gaussian MIMO-ISI channels where channel taps and spatial noise covariance are unknown.
method: The authors approximate the frequency response by block-constant matrices, exploit affine matched log-likelihoods in a common sufficient statistic, and bound competitor probabilities using density estimates over symmetric neighborhoods.
result: The proposed decoder attains the ensemble-average error exponent of informed maximum-likelihood decoding for fixed channels and growing-memory channels, with a Gaussian channel comparison transferring the result to the original channel.
conclusion: The work provides a universal decoding scheme with optimal error exponents for Gaussian MIMO-ISI channels under stated frequency-variation and energy conditions.

title: Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing In Large Language Models
authors: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
tldr: The paper introduces Logit Laundering, an inference-time logit-reshaping framework that suppresses watermark signals to evade data-use auditing of LLMs while preserving model utility.
motivation: Non-compliant LLM providers may train on unauthorized copyrighted data yet wish to avoid detection by watermark-based data-use auditors, and systematic adversarial study of such evasion is lacking.
method: A logit reshaping module with a plug-in statistical bias estimator suppresses watermark-induced statistical signals in the logit space without changing model parameters, complemented by a confidence-aware scaling module that adaptively calibrates suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence.
result: Extensive evaluations show the attack evades multiple state-of-the-art auditing methods, substantially attenuating detectable signals while maintaining downstream task performance.
conclusion: The work exposes a serious vulnerability in current LLM data-use auditing and motivates the development of more robust watermarking and auditing schemes.

title: Optimal Regret For Profit Maximization In Bilateral Trade
authors: Matteo Castiglioni, Anna Lunghi, Alberto Marchesi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret [MATH] against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.
tldr: The paper designs a regret-optimal learning algorithm for repeated bilateral trade where an intermediary posts prices to a seller and a buyer with unknown joint valuations, showing the two-dimensional problem attains the same regret rate as one-dimensional dynamic pricing.
motivation: Learning to profit from trade requires simultaneously learning both the seller's acceptance threshold and the buyer's willingness to pay from only binary trade-feasibility feedback, and it was unclear whether this two-sided learning incurs a curse of dimensionality in regret.
method: The authors formulate repeated bilateral trade as an online learning problem with bandit-style feedback (only whether trade occurred) and construct an algorithm that achieves regret matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical one-dimensional dynamic pricing lower bound against the best fixed price pair.
result: The proposed algorithm attains the optimal one-dimensional regret rate despite the two-dimensional price space, proving that learning both sides of the market is no harder than learning one side.
conclusion: The classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the open question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality persists in arbitrarily high dimensions.

title: Recurrent And Rigid Multipliers On Commutative Banach Algebras. The Fourier Algebra
authors: Mar\'ia J. Beltr\'an-Meneu, Jorga Galindo, Enrique Jord\'a
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study recurrence, rigidity and uniform rigidity of multipliers on semisimple commutative Banach algebras. For a power-bounded multiplier [MATH] on a Tauberian, self-adjoint algebra [MATH], we show that [MATH] satisfies each of these properties if and only if the multiplication operator on [MATH] induced by the Gelfand transform of [MATH] does. One consequence of our analysis is that, if [MATH] is [MATH]-compact, then recurrence implies rigidity for such multipliers. We examine in detail the multipliers of the Fourier algebra [MATH]. In particular, we show that recurrence of a multiplier of [MATH] is equivalent to recurrence of the corresponding multiplier on [MATH] when the connected components of [MATH] are open. For multipliers that are not power bounded, a flexible construction based on chains of compact subgroups of a locally compact abelian group [MATH] produces multipliers of [MATH] that are rigid but not uniformly rigid, and multipliers that are recurrent but not rigid, such that in each case the corresponding multiplier on [MATH] is uniformly rigid. Via the Fourier-Stieltjes transform, these results describe the recurrence and rigidity properties of convolution operators on [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies recurrence, rigidity, and uniform rigidity of multipliers on semisimple commutative Banach algebras, with a detailed application to the Fourier algebra.
motivation: The authors aim to understand dynamical properties of multipliers on commutative Banach algebras and transfer these properties via Gelfand transforms and Fourier-Stieltjes transforms.
method: They prove equivalences between recurrence/rigidity of power-bounded multipliers and the corresponding multiplication operators induced by Gelfand transforms, and construct examples using chains of compact subgroups of locally compact abelian groups for non-power-bounded multipliers.
result: For Tauberian self-adjoint algebras, the properties are shown to be equivalent under power-boundedness; for the Fourier algebra, recurrence of a multiplier is characterized under open connected components, and rigid-but-not-uniformly-rigid and recurrent-but-not-rigid examples are constructed.
conclusion: The work provides a functional-analytic characterization of recurrence and rigidity for multipliers on commutative Banach algebras, especially the Fourier algebra, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: NotaryMark: Multi-Bit Watermarking For Black-Box DatasetUsage Auditing In Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
authors: Xinyi Yu, Linkang Du, Zhou Su, Min Chen, Yuntao Wang, Zhikun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) models increasingly require data, more publicly available yet licensed data is being harvested and used without authorization. Although several previous studies have proposed watermarking methods for dataset copyright auditing, their applicability to the text-to-image (T2I) setting remains notably limited. The core drawback is that watermarks embedded by existing techniques are often treated as noise and are gradually filtered out and attenuated during the latent noising-denoising process of diffusion model training. We propose NotaryMark, to our knowledge the first multi-bit watermarking method specifically designed for black-box auditing of T2I training dataset use. The core idea of NotaryMark is to align the watermark with the latent denoising of diffusion models, thereby overcoming the signal decay that plagues existing multi-bit methods during sampling. We evaluate NotaryMark across three datasets and three diffusion models spanning watermark capacities from 8 to 1024 bits. With a watermark capacity below 32 bits, it achieves a high average bit accuracy of 0.85-0.90. With a watermark capacity exceeding 32 bits, it maintains bit accuracy between 0.67 and 0.80, consistently outperforming existing multi-bit watermark methods whose bit accuracy is around 0.42-0.60. Furthermore, we design a voting-based aggregation scheme to boost the bit accuracy with a modest budget of 30 queries. Building on this, we incorporate error-correcting codes to enable reliable decoding and tracing of the embedded identifier information. Robustness evaluation against fifteen evasion attacks spanning seven categories shows that NotaryMark remains robust under most evaluated settings, while stronger attacks generally suppress watermark evidence only at the cost of substantial utility degradation, demonstrating its practical reliability against malicious tampering.
tldr: NotaryMark is a multi-bit watermarking method for black-box auditing of text-to-image diffusion model training dataset usage.
motivation: Licensed public data is increasingly harvested for generative AI training without authorization, and existing dataset watermarking methods are poorly suited to text-to-image diffusion models because watermarks decay during latent denoising.
method: The authors align the watermark with the latent denoising process of diffusion models, use a voting-based aggregation scheme over multiple queries, and incorporate error-correcting codes for reliable identifier decoding.
result: Across three datasets and three diffusion models, NotaryMark achieves 0.85–0.90 bit accuracy for capacities below 32 bits and 0.67–0.80 for higher capacities, outperforming existing multi-bit watermarks, while remaining robust to most of fifteen evasion attacks.
conclusion: NotaryMark provides a practical multi-bit watermarking approach for auditing unauthorized text-to-image dataset usage, though it is outside the user's quantum information research scope.

title: Optimal Feedback Control Of The Fokker-Planck Equation For An Sirs Epidemic Model
authors: Souvik Roy Christian Parkinson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a Fokker--Planck feedback control framework for a stochastic susceptible--infected--recovered--susceptible (SIRS) epidemic model with three intervention mechanisms targeting disease transmission, loss of immunity, and recovery. The interventions are formulated as space- and time-dependent feedback controls that influence both the drift and diffusion coefficients of the underlying stochastic differential equations, allowing control of the probability distribution of epidemic states. We investigate the existence of optimal controls and derive first-order necessary optimality conditions involving a forward Fokker--Planck equation, a backward adjoint equation, and a Hamiltonian minimization condition. For numerical approximation, we combine a Chang--Cooper discretization of the diagonal drift--diffusion terms with a finite-difference treatment of cross-diffusion and a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) algorithm for computing the optimal feedback policies. We also examine sufficient-decrease and convergence properties of the SQH iteration. Numerical experiments consider four epidemiological objectives involving cumulative infection burden, infection-threshold exceedance, terminal susceptible population, and a combination of running and terminal costs. The resulting feedback policies exhibit distinct spatial and temporal structures depending on the epidemiological objective. Monte Carlo simulations of the underlying stochastic system illustrate that the optimized interventions can substantially reduce infection growth and undesirable epidemic outcomes relative to uncontrolled dynamics. The proposed framework provides a distribution-based approach to stochastic epidemic control that integrates mathematical analysis, numerical optimization, and state-dependent intervention design.
tldr: The paper develops a Fokker-Planck feedback control framework for a stochastic SIRS epidemic model with three intervention mechanisms, deriving optimality conditions and solving them numerically via a Chang-Cooper/SQH scheme.
motivation: Stochastic epidemic dynamics are governed by distributions of states rather than single trajectories, so interventions should be designed at the level of the probability distribution; the authors seek a principled distribution-based control methodology.
method: Space- and time-dependent feedback controls modify both drift and diffusion of the underlying SDEs; first-order necessary optimality conditions couple a forward Fokker-Planck equation, a backward adjoint equation, and a Hamiltonian minimization, solved with Chang-Cooper discretization of diagonal drift-diffusion, finite differences for cross-diffusion, and a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian algorithm.
result: Existence of optimal controls and convergence properties of the SQH iteration are established, and four epidemiological objectives (cumulative infection burden, threshold exceedance, terminal susceptible population, combined costs) yield distinct spatio-temporal feedback structures; Monte Carlo simulations show substantially reduced infection growth versus uncontrolled dynamics.
conclusion: Distribution-level Fokker-Planck feedback control is a viable and effective tool for designing state-dependent epidemic interventions, integrating mathematical analysis, numerical optimization, and intervention design.

title: Disjointness Preserving Operators On K\"{o}the-Banach Spaces
authors: Iryna Krasikova, Mikhail Popov, Beata Randrianantoanina
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A well-known result of Abramovich says that if [MATH], [MATH] are rearrangement invariant Banach spaces on a finite atomless measure space such that [MATH] has an absolutely continuous norm and [MATH], then there are no nonzero disjointness preserving bounded linear operators [MATH]. We obtain an analogue of this result in the setting of general K\"{o}the-Banach spaces. Specifically, we identify a sufficient condition on K\"{o}the-Banach spaces [MATH], [MATH] on finite atomless measure spaces that implies that there are no nonzero disjointness preserving bounded linear operators [MATH]. Consequently, by a representation theorem for regular operators due to O.~Maslyuchenko, Mykhaylyuk and the second named author, this condition implies that every regular linear operator [MATH] is narrow. As an application, we obtain that if [MATH], then every regular linear operator [MATH] is narrow. The latter may be seen as an analogue of the classical Pitt compactness theorem.
tldr: The paper characterizes when no nonzero disjointness preserving bounded linear operators exist between general Köthe-Banach spaces over atomless measure spaces, showing all regular operators are narrow.
motivation: Abramovich's classical result rules out nonzero disjointness preserving operators between rearrangement invariant Banach spaces under an inclusion condition; the authors seek an analogue beyond the rearrangement invariant setting.
method: Pure functional analysis: a sufficient condition on pairs of Köthe-Banach spaces is identified, combined with a representation theorem for regular operators due to Maslyuchenko, Mykhaylyuk and Popov.
result: The condition implies every regular linear operator between the spaces is narrow, yielding, for instance, that when one space is L1 every regular operator is narrow—an analogue of Pitt's compactness theorem.
conclusion: The work extends Abramovich-type disjointness results to Köthe-Banach spaces and connects narrowness of regular operators to classical compactness phenomena.

title: On Optimal Convergence Rates For Parametrized Variational Problems With Applications To Nonlocal Models
authors: Zhaolong Han, James Scott, Xiaochuan Tian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an abstract variational framework for convergence rates of parametrized problems and their Galerkin approximations, with applications to nonlocal diffusion. The main objective is to quantify modeling and discretization errors in terms of the nonlocal horizon, the mesh size, the Sobolev regularity of the local solution, and the compatibility of boundary data. We establish error estimates in energy and [MATH] norms and develop an adaptation of the Aubin--Nitsche argument that uses regularity of the limiting local dual problem. This approach yields improved [MATH] estimates without requiring additional regularity of the nonlocal dual solutions, including for integrable kernels. We apply the framework to two constant-horizon nonlocal Laplacians with exterior boundary data and to heterogeneous localization models with classical Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions. The resulting estimates provide quantitative guarantees of asymptotic compatibility and improve existing error bounds under weaker regularity assumptions. Numerical experiments illustrate the convergence rates and examine the sharpness of the estimates.
tldr: An abstract variational framework for deriving convergence rates of parametrized problems and their Galerkin approximations, applied to nonlocal diffusion models.
motivation: Nonlocal models require quantitative control of modeling error (set by the horizon) and discretization error (set by mesh size), but existing error bounds often demand strong regularity of nonlocal dual solutions.
method: The authors build an abstract variational convergence framework, establishing energy and L2 error estimates and adapting the Aubin–Nitsche argument using regularity of the limiting local dual problem, applied to constant-horizon nonlocal Laplacians with exterior data and to heterogeneous localization models.
result: Improved L2 estimates are obtained without extra regularity of nonlocal dual solutions, including for integrable kernels, giving quantitative asymptotic compatibility under weaker assumptions, confirmed by numerical experiments probing sharpness.
conclusion: The framework yields sharper, more broadly applicable convergence guarantees for nonlocal-to-local asymptotics and Galerkin discretizations of parametrized variational problems.

title: Asymptotic Stability Of High-index Saddle Dynamics
authors: Baoming Shi, Lei Zhang, Xiangcheng Zheng, Shangqin Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-index saddle dynamics (HiSD) has been extensively adopted to compute saddle points of arbitrary index, with various applications such as constructing solution landscapes of complex systems. In this work, we prove the asymptotic stability of various HiSD methods, including the idealized, perturbed, and coupled HiSD methods, as well as their momentum-accelerated variants. The analysis is Jacobian-free and thus compensates for the linear stability analysis in the literature. The results not only provide specific characterizations for the convergence rate and the basin of attraction, but also reveal intrinsic correlations among dynamics in the coupled HiSD. Theoretical results are substantiated by numerical experiments.
tldr: The paper proves asymptotic stability for high-index saddle dynamics (HiSD) methods, including idealized, perturbed, coupled, and momentum-accelerated variants, using a Jacobian-free analysis.
motivation: HiSD is widely used to compute saddle points of arbitrary index and construct solution landscapes of complex systems, but existing stability analyses were limited to linear (Jacobian-based) treatments that miss global convergence properties.
method: The authors derive asymptotic stability proofs for several HiSD variants without invoking the Jacobian, yielding characterizations of convergence rates and basins of attraction, plus correlations among coupled HiSD dynamics, supported by numerical experiments.
result: Explicit convergence-rate and basin-of-attraction characterizations are obtained for idealized, perturbed, coupled, and momentum-accelerated HiSD, revealing intrinsic correlations between the coupled dynamics.
conclusion: The Jacobian-free stability framework extends and complements prior linear stability analysis and provides practical guarantees for HiSD-based saddle-point search in complex systems.

title: Hecke Algebras For Minimal Equicontinuous Cantor Actions
authors: Pablo Lummerzheim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work we extend the concept of Hecke algebras to a pair of a separable infinite profinite group and a closed core-free subgroup. Motivated by applications to minimal equicontinuous Cantor actions, which are characterized by such pairs, we characterize isometric *-algebra isomorphisms between such Hecke algebras by showing that they always arise as Koopman operators of homeomorphisms between the double coset spaces combined with the multiplication by some character. We then prove that two minimal equicontinuous Cantor actions with isometric isomorphic Hecke algebras have the same Steinitz order. We provide examples including the infinite dihedral group and the Grigorchuk group.
tldr: The paper generalizes Hecke algebras to pairs of a profinite group with a core-free subgroup and characterizes their isometric *-algebra isomorphisms via Koopman operators on double coset spaces.
motivation: Minimal equicontinuous Cantor actions are classified by such (profinite group, core-free subgroup) pairs, so a Hecke-algebra framework offers an algebraic invariant for studying these topological dynamical systems.
method: The authors extend the Hecke algebra construction to the profinite setting, prove that isometric *-algebra isomorphisms arise from Koopman operators of homeomorphisms of double coset spaces combined with a character, and derive invariance of the Steinitz order.
result: Isomorphic Hecke algebras imply equal Steinitz order for the corresponding minimal equicontinuous Cantor actions, with worked examples for the infinite dihedral group and the Grigorchuk group.
conclusion: Hecke algebras provide a useful algebraic-combinatorial invariant for equicontinuous Cantor dynamics, though the work is purely mathematical with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Faster Treasure Hunt Via Strongly Universal Exploration With Polylogarithmic Overhead
authors: Qin Xin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study deterministic exploration and delayed-activation treasure hunt in anonymous undirected port-labeled graphs with incoming-port information. From polynomial-time constructible ordinary universal exploration sequences of length \(O(n^c)\) for a fixed regular degree, we construct a single infinite strongly universal exploration sequence with cover time \(O(n^c\log^2n)\). Summable dyadic insertion schedules yield the sharper bound \(O_\eps(n^c\log n(\log\log n)^{1+\eps})\) for every fixed \(\eps>0\), together with refinements at every fixed iterated-logarithm depth. The proof combines reversible excursions, neutral guards and an arbitrary-window argument that treats both orientations simultaneously. For this recurrence, uniform linear expansion is equivalent to convergence of the normalized period sum. Exact counting identities also permit direct instruction access. With a logspace ordinary generator, table-free enumeration of decreasing scale paths computes instruction \(t\) using \(O(\log(t+2))\) working bits and time polynomial in \(t\). The earlier polynomial-slack bounds follow as corollaries. A local cubic simulation extends the treasure-hunt application to arbitrary-degree graphs, with the \(2m\)-vertex replacement size included explicitly in the bound.
tldr: The paper constructs strongly universal exploration sequences with polylogarithmic overhead to improve deterministic graph exploration and delayed-activation treasure hunt algorithms.
motivation: Deterministic exploration and treasure hunt in anonymous port-labeled graphs are central problems in distributed computing; existing universal exploration sequences incur polynomial slack that the authors aim to reduce.
method: Starting from polynomial-time constructible ordinary universal exploration sequences of length O(n^c) for fixed regular degree, the authors build a single infinite strongly universal exploration sequence using reversible excursions, neutral guards, an arbitrary-window argument, and summable dyadic insertion schedules, plus a local cubic simulation for arbitrary-degree graphs.
result: They obtain cover time O(n^c log^2 n), sharpened to O_eps(n^c log n (log log n)^{1+eps}), along with logspace table-free instruction access using O(log(t+2)) working bits and time polynomial in t.
conclusion: The construction yields improved polynomial-slack bounds for deterministic exploration and treasure hunt, and extends to arbitrary-degree graphs via a cubic simulation with explicit vertex-replacement overhead.

title: Beyond A Single Commit: Anchor-Guided Reconstruction Of Multi-Commit Patches
authors: Jialiang Dong, Willy Susilo, Xu Gai, Liuhuo Wan, Chao Zhang, Elisa Bertino, Siqi Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patch identification plays a critical role in software security by linking reported vulnerabilities and the corresponding fixes, enabling reliable vulnerability analysis, mitigation, and automated security tool development. As software systems evolve in complexity, vulnerability remediation has increasingly shifted from single-commit fixes to multi-commit fixing processes. Although many studies have been proposed to identify fixing commits associated with target vulnerabilities automatically, they often suffer from inaccurate semantic analysis or excessive workload for language models. These limitations reduce both the effectiveness and comprehensiveness of fixing commit identification. To improve patch identification, we propose an effective and comprehensive patch identification framework, HARPOON, which not only enhances the accuracy of identifying individual fixing commits, but also investigates dependencies among commits to achieve comprehensive commit recognition for target vulnerabilities. Experimental results show that HARPOON significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches. HARPOON successfully identified 895 vulnerability patches that were not previously maintained in public vulnerability databases. Among them, 663 are previously unrecorded fixes associated with 323 CRITICAL- or HIGH-severity vulnerabilities.
tldr: HARPOON is a framework for identifying vulnerability-fixing commits, including multi-commit patches, by using anchor-guided reconstruction and commit dependency analysis.
motivation: Vulnerability remediation increasingly spans multiple commits, and existing automated fixing-commit identification methods suffer from inaccurate semantic analysis and high language-model workload.
method: The authors propose HARPOON, an anchor-guided reconstruction framework that improves individual fixing-commit identification and models dependencies among commits to recognize comprehensive multi-commit patches.
result: HARPOON outperforms state-of-the-art approaches and identified 895 previously unmaintained vulnerability patches, including 663 unrecorded fixes for 323 CRITICAL- or HIGH-severity vulnerabilities.
conclusion: The work advances software-security patch identification but has no direct connection to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Federated Forensics: Jurisdictional Constraints As A Design Driver For Multi-agency Federated Learning
authors: Aruna Withanage, Jessica Herrmann, Hudan Studiawan, Frank Breitinger
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.
tldr: The paper proposes 'Federated Forensics,' a three-layer reference architecture for cross-jurisdictional federated learning in digital forensic investigations, with a policy gate at the jurisdictional border that blocks restricted model updates.
motivation: Digital forensic investigations increasingly span national borders, and law enforcement agencies want to jointly train analytical models without centralizing sensitive data, yet existing federated learning frameworks do not enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability constraints such multi-agency work demands.
method: The authors derive seven requirements for forensic federated learning, design a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer sits at a jurisdictional border and can locally use but not export a model update, and implement a prototype evaluated on a malware-family classification task.
result: The policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under the current compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below the unrestricted case.
conclusion: Treating jurisdictional constraints as a first-class design driver enables compliant multi-agency federated forensics that preserves most of the accuracy benefit of unrestricted collaboration.

title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction On Tabular Data
authors: Seyma Selcan Magara, Hanru Zhang, Fatme El Zahraa Hamad, Nico Pfeifer, Mete Akg\"un
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data. Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.
tldr: Cutpurse is an explanation-guided model-extraction attack on tabular classifiers that separates attribution from coordinate channels and shows self-computed query grids substitute for leaked explainer bin edges.
motivation: Practitioners assume explanation APIs raise model-extraction risk, but it is unclear whether explanations leak model-specific information or merely provide convenient query coordinates, so the authors disentangle these two roles.
method: Across six datasets and five target model families, the authors split Lime/Shap explanations into an attribution channel (feature rankings) and a coordinate channel (candidate feature values), then compare attacker-side grids with service-provided bin edges and build the Cutpurse attack combining a self-computed grid, diverse query generation, and boundary search.
result: Attribution rankings give no systematic extraction advantage, while Lime bin edges (quantiles of the explainer's background data, not model properties) can boost fidelity by up to 41 percentage points, and Cutpurse recovers 16.3 points on continuous-feature targets even when bin edges are withheld, beating the published undefended attack by 7.0 points.
conclusion: Withholding default Lime bin edges does not prevent effective extraction under in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, same-family surrogate assumptions, though the findings are limited to default Lime/Shap configurations for tabular classifiers.

title: Raytracing And Quantifying The Inferior Mirage
authors: Nathan Hagen, Lucas Reyes Bentancor, Kakeru Tanaka, Norimasa Hanaya, Momo Shoda, Hiroki Maki, Takuma Ando, Keisaku Yoshizawa, Kayo Suzuki, Yume Yamada, Asana Kumakura
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using custom raytracing code, we explore several features of the inferior mirage that are not widely discussed, such as the blurring in the mirage image, and what happens to the light in the direct image region that is replaced by the mirage image. The raytracing model also clarifies how to quantify the mirage, and we provide expressions to calculate the angular extent of the mirage under given thermal conditions and measurement geometry.
tldr: The paper uses custom raytracing to model and quantify optical features of the inferior mirage, including blurring and light behavior in the direct-image region.
motivation: Several features of the inferior mirage, such as image blurring and the fate of light in the replaced direct-image region, are not widely discussed in the literature.
method: Custom raytracing code is used to simulate inferior mirage formation under varying thermal conditions and measurement geometries.
result: The model clarifies how to quantify the mirage and provides expressions for calculating its angular extent from thermal and geometric parameters.
conclusion: The work offers a clearer raytracing-based characterization of inferior mirages and practical formulas for their angular extent.

title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods For Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence Via Increment Sharing
authors: Bhavika Balani, Taeho Yoon, Nicolas Loizou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.
tldr: This paper develops compressed and variance-reduced variants of Per-Player Local SGD for multiplayer federated learning, proving exact convergence by sharing local strategy increments rather than full strategies.
motivation: Multiplayer Federated Learning extends federated learning to rational clients seeking game equilibria, but the baseline PEARL-SGD does not extend cleanly to compressed communication because directly compressing strategies can prevent convergence.
method: The authors reformulate PEARL-SGD so players communicate local strategy increments, then introduce compressed C-PEARL-SGD and variance-reduced PEARL-SVRG/C-PEARL-SVRG variants, with convergence guarantees derived from a unified parametric inequality.
result: Increment sharing preserves exact convergence under compression, and numerical experiments including distributed spectrum sensing show practical benefits over vanilla PEARL-SGD.
conclusion: The proposed compressed per-player local methods make multiplayer federated learning communication-efficient while retaining convergence guarantees, but the work is entirely in classical optimization and distributed learning.

title: Vector Lyapunov Functions For Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
authors: Ilya Kolmanovsky Torbj{\o}rn Cunis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonconvex constrained optimization problems are commonly solved by a Newton method for necessary conditions (sequential linear/quadratic programming) or a barrier reformulation (interior-point methods). We present a vector Lyapunov analysis for Newton-type algorithms based on constraint violation and optimality of the primal solutions to a sequence of approximate optimization problems. We thus prove local stability and convergence by constructing a strict Lyapunov function for the primal solution.
tldr: The paper develops a vector Lyapunov framework for analyzing the local stability and convergence of Newton-type methods for nonconvex constrained optimization.
motivation: Nonconvex constrained optimization is typically tackled by sequential linear/quadratic programming or interior-point methods, but a unified stability analysis based on constraint violation and primal optimality is lacking.
method: The authors construct a vector Lyapunov function using constraint violation and the optimality of primal solutions to a sequence of approximate problems, then apply it to Newton-type algorithms.
result: They prove local stability and convergence of the primal solution under suitable conditions via a strict Lyapunov function.
conclusion: Vector Lyapunov analysis provides a rigorous stability framework for Newton-type constrained optimization algorithms, complementing standard SQP and interior-point perspectives.

title: Second-order Optimality Conditions For $c^{1,1}$ Sparsity Constrained Optimization Problems Via Disjunctive Programming
authors: Luu Thi Thu Huyen, Liguo Jiao, Nguyen van Tuyen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for a class of [MATH] sparsity constrained optimization problems via a disjunctive programming approach. More precisely, by utilizing the limiting/Mordukhovich second-order subdifferential of the associated Lagrangian function, we establish new second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for local optimal solutions. These results are derived under mild assumptions and extend several existing results in the literature. In addition, we apply our theoretical developments to sparse multiobjective optimization problems and derive second-order optimality conditions for efficient solutions.
tldr: The paper derives second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for C^{1,1} sparsity-constrained optimization problems using a disjunctive programming approach.
motivation: Sparsity-constrained optimization is challenging due to nonconvexity and disjunctive structure, and higher-order optimality conditions are needed beyond first-order theory.
method: The authors use limiting/Mordukhovich second-order subdifferentials of the Lagrangian and a disjunctive programming reformulation to establish optimality conditions under mild assumptions.
result: New second-order necessary and sufficient conditions for local optimal solutions are obtained, extending existing results, and are applied to sparse multiobjective optimization.
conclusion: The work advances nonsmooth optimization theory for sparsity constraints but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: AutoPYara: Next-Gen Yara Rule Generator For Malware Family Clustering
authors: Mabon Ninan, Nhat Nguyen, Soumyajyoti Dutta, Sidharth Anil, Marcus Botacin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.
tldr: AutoPYara is an open-source Python tool that improves automatic YARA rule generation for clustering and detecting malware families.
motivation: Millions of malware variants require fast clustering for incident response, but existing automatic rule generation (AutoYara) degrades on realistic datasets due to intra-family diversity and noisy clustering.
method: The authors introduce similarity-hashing-based cluster centroid selection and an improved heuristic that estimates subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data, released as a pip-installable package.
result: AutoPYara increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points, reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, and improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10% relative to AutoYara.
conclusion: The proposed tool produces more robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical malware-analysis settings.

title: Jev As An Llm Safety Guardrail: An Empirical Study Of Input Filtering, Selective Output Review, And Over-Refusal
authors: Bhaskar Krishnamachari Olivia Cognetti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: External safety filters can prevent unsafe requests from reaching a large language model (LLM), but may also reject legitimate queries. We present an end-to-end empirical evaluation of Jev, a probabilistic decision model, as a safety guardrail for a Qwen2.5-1.5B-based pipeline. Three configurations are compared on 970 benchmark prompts: an unfiltered LLM, Jev input filtering, and tiered Jev input filtering with selective output review. Across 720 prompts labeled harmful (520 AdvBench and 200 XSTest-unsafe), the fraction recorded as answered decreases from 527/720 (73.2%) without filtering to 17/720 (2.4%) with input filtering. On 250 XSTest-safe prompts, however, non-answer/refusal increases from 3/250 (1.2%) to 27/250 (10.8%). Tiered filtering yields 40/720 (5.6%) harmful-prompt answers and 10/250 (4.0%) benign-prompt refusals, with 79/970 (8.1%) of prompts requiring output review. Joint optimization of the tiered thresholds improves macro-F1 from 0.9351 to 0.9512, while reducing harmful-prompt answers and output-review frequency at the same benign-refusal rate. Matched-budget comparisons reveal modest additional gains over a retuned single gate on the evaluation data, although these gains are not consistently observed on a held-out split.
tldr: This paper empirically evaluates the Jev probabilistic decision model as an external safety guardrail for a Qwen2.5-1.5B-based LLM pipeline, comparing input filtering and selective output review on harmful and benign prompts.
motivation: External safety filters can block unsafe LLM requests but may also over-refuse legitimate queries, so the authors aim to quantify the trade-off between harmful-prompt suppression and benign-prompt refusal.
method: They compare three configurations on 970 benchmark prompts: an unfiltered LLM, Jev input filtering, and tiered Jev input filtering with selective output review, using AdvBench and XSTest-unsafe/safe labels and tuning tiered thresholds for macro-F1.
result: Input filtering reduces recorded answers on harmful prompts from 73.2% to 2.4% while increasing benign refusals from 1.2% to 10.8%; tiered filtering reaches 5.6% harmful-prompt answers and 4.0% benign refusals with 8.1% of prompts requiring output review, and joint threshold optimization improves macro-F1 from 0.9351 to 0.9512.
conclusion: Jev-based filtering can substantially suppress harmful LLM responses, but gains over a retuned single gate are modest and not consistently observed on a held-out split, highlighting the need for careful evaluation of over-refusal and generalization.

title: Authorization Drift In Llm Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance In Multi-Step Tool Use
authors: Chuxue Cao, Jingru Zeng, Boqin Yin, Yujin Zhou, Yidan Huang, Sujin Chen, Jinluan Yang, Haoran Li, Yike Guo, Sirui Han
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.
tldr: The paper introduces an LLM-agent benchmark for measuring authorization drift, where agents exceed permitted data, tool, scope, or time boundaries while pursuing user goals.
motivation: LLM agents can overstep authorization boundaries even without adversarial prompting, creating privacy and security risks that are not captured by existing capability benchmarks.
method: The authors formalize authorization drift and build the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB), using Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis to validate tasks with real agent rollouts across multiple domains, models, and frameworks.
result: Across 25,207 trajectories and 13 LLMs, more capable models show higher drift rates (0.43–0.61), though 86.18% of tasks have at least one clean-success trajectory; drift is persistent and often driven by early data over-collection.
conclusion: Authorization drift is a measurable and avoidable LLM-agent safety failure, with legal implications across jurisdictions, but it is unrelated to quantum information science or the defined research directions.

title: Predicting Next-week Viirs Fire Detections In Bolivia: A Reproducible Benchmark With Temporal And Geographic Evaluation
authors: Victor Hugo Cuellar Flores
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weekly detection forecasts could help prioritize fire monitoring across Bolivia. We estimate the probability of at least one fire detection by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite in each 0.05-degree cell during the following 7 days. Primary models were fixed before test scoring. Calibrated LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision-tree model, reaches 2023-2025 temporal-test average precision (AP) of 0.323 (95% block-bootstrap interval 0.222-0.383), compared with 0.167 for climatology and 0.143 for persistence. Its paired AP gain over climatology is 0.1567 (0.0998-0.2179). A separately selected geographic model reaches AP 0.384 versus 0.181 for persistence in regions excluded from fitting. In the temporal-test population, reviewing the highest-ranked 5% and 10% of eligible area would have covered 38.4% and 55.8% of cell-weeks with detections. Probabilities still overestimate detection frequency in the highest-probability group.
